title: Shell stitch
subtitle: Five trebles into one stitch, fanning open from a shared base
excerpt: A shell is five (or any odd number of) trebles worked into the same stitch, spreading outward from the shared base. The defining stitch of shell-stitch blankets and edgings, and the base unit of dozens of pattern combinations.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volumes 1-3 (Internet Archive). Shell stitch in traditional British blanket and edging patterns. Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), shell pattern constructions.
heroPrompt: A swatch of shell stitch in cream DK cotton showing the fan-shaped shells above a row of double crochet, the five trebles clearly visible fanning out from each shell base. Natural linen background.

glossaryTerms.definition: Five (or any odd number of) trebles worked into the same base stitch, fanning open. The legs share a base; the tops spread across. Abbreviated shell or sh. The building block of shell-stitch blanket patterns.

content.text: fans five trebles from a single point. All five go into the same stitch, each worked as a normal complete treble. They spread across the fabric above, five side-by-side tops above one shared base, so the shape looks exactly like a scallop shell.
Identify the base stitch (usually a chain space or a stitch the pattern designates as the shell point).
Work 5 complete trebles, all into the same stitch or space. Each treble is finished normally before starting the next.
The five trebles sit side by side with their tops evenly spread. That is the complete shell.
Foundation: ch 24 (multiple of 6, plus 3 for turning). Turn.
Row 1 (base row): ch 3 (counts as first tr), *skip 2 ch, 5tr shell in next ch, skip 2 ch, tr in next ch; repeat from * across (4 shells + edge trs). Turn.
Row 2: ch 3, *5tr shell into the 3rd (centre) tr of each shell below, tr into the single tr between shells; repeat from * across. Turn.
Repeat row 2 for the shell stitch pattern.

attrs.title: The centre treble is the next row's shell point
attrs.body: In a shell-stitch pattern, the next row's shell always goes into the centre (middle, 3rd of 5) treble of the shell below. If you lose track of the centre, count: edge, 1, 2, 3-centre, 4, 5, edge. The shell goes into position 3.

items.symptom: The shells are lopsided — some lean left, some right
items.cause: The shell point is not centered on the previous row's shell.
items.fix: Always place the new shell into the exact centre treble of the shell below. Count the trebles in each shell before starting the next row.

items.symptom: The edge stitches are not aligning properly
items.cause: The pattern multiple is off by one, or the turning chain was not counted correctly on the first row.
items.fix: Restart with the correct foundation chain (a multiple of 6 for a 5-tr shell pattern, plus 3 for the turning chain). Count the chain before turning.

items.symptom: The shell looks too open or too closed
items.cause: Tension mismatch — the trebles within the shell are either too loose or too tight.
items.fix: Aim for even tension on all five trebles. The shell should fan symmetrically: the outer trebles lean slightly out, the centre treble stands straight.

content.text: The fan stitch is a shell variant worked into a larger base (seven or nine trebles into a chain space rather than a single stitch). The granny cluster is a three-treble cluster equivalent of the shell concept applied to motif construction. Both appear in the Stitches library.
